title: The Atlas of Manchester's mill district
premise: In 1842, August 'Gussie' Vane works the type cases in her father's print shop on the Ancoats mill district's only bridge, cutting type by day and secretly setting pamphlets for the Chartists by night. When the bridge closes for winter repairs and the mills lock out their workers, the shop becomes a refuge, a target, and a printing press for a revolution nobody planned. As the ice thickens on the river and the magistrates close in, Gussie must choose between protecting her father's fragile legacy and printing the truth that could destroy them both — and she finishes the run the night the ice breaks, letting the river carry the evidence away while she stays to face the consequences.
about_author: Cyrus Reyes is the pen name of a former letterpress apprentice who spent a decade restoring Victorian printing equipment in northern England before turning to fiction. Their work draws on family stories of mill-town printers who risked everything for the freedom of the press.

chapters.title: The Weight of Lead
chapters.summary: Gussie Vane's POV. A working day in the Vane print shop: sorting type, minding her father's tremor, keeping her head down as mill hands grumble about wages. She notices the first Chartists' bills pasted near the bridge. Emotional beat: quiet competence masking a restless hunger for something more than invisibility.

chapters.title: Ink Under the Nails
chapters.summary: Gussie's POV. A stranger with a Manchester accent and clean cuffs commissions five hundred handbills, paying in silver. Her father accepts; Gussie recognizes the phrasing as Chartist. She says nothing. Emotional beat: the first small compromise, the thrill and shame of complicity.

chapters.title: The Bridge Closes
chapters.summary: Gussie's POV. Scaffolding rises on the bridge; the only road out shuts for the season, and with it the mail, the coal carts, the escape routes. The district becomes an island. Emotional beat: claustrophobia — the realization that the walls she hid behind have become a cage.

chapters.title: The Lockout
chapters.summary: Mill worker Ellen Brack's POV. The mills turn out four thousand hands without warning; families queue at the relief committee. Ellen recognizes Gussie from the shop and asks, plainly, if the Vanes will print for the workers. Emotional beat: dignity under humiliation, and the first pull on Gussie's conscience.

chapters.title: What Father Cut
chapters.summary: Gussie's POV, with a flashback to her mother. She finds a hidden drawer of her dead mother's radical woodcuts from the 1819 Peterloo years — proof the family was never neutral. Emotional beat: inheritance of a secret she never asked to carry.

chapters.title: Five Hundred Handbills
chapters.summary: Gussie's POV. She prints the workers' handbill at night, alone, telling herself it's charity. Ellen collects them wrapped in shawls. A constable lingers outside the shop. Emotional beat: fear braided with exhilaration — invisibility is already gone.

chapters.title: The Man with Clean Cuffs
chapters.summary: The stranger — solicitor's clerk Nathaniel Quill — returns, revealing he is organizing a district-wide strike committee and wants the Vanes to print a weekly. Gussie's father refuses; Gussie hears herself volunteering. Emotional beat: the dangerous pleasure of being asked, finally, to matter.

chapters.title: Ice on the Irwell
chapters.summary: Ellen's POV. The river freezes; hunger deepens; a child dies of fever in the cellar dwellings. Ellen's brother wants to smash the shop windows as traitors' property. Emotional beat: the movement's anger turning inward, testing whether solidarity can hold.

chapters.title: The First Number
chapters.summary: Gussie's POV. The first issue of The Bridge, the strike weekly, rolls off the press — set in her mother's reclaimed type. Distribution through mill girls and chapel deacons. Emotional beat: authorship; Gussie's words, not her father's, in public for the first time.

chapters.title: A Reward for Names
chapters.summary: Magistrate's clerk POV. The authorities offer ten pounds for the printer of The Bridge; informers circle the district. Gussie's father, terrified, burns a proof and forbids her to continue. Emotional beat: the first open rupture between duty to family and duty to the work.

chapters.title: Nathaniel's Bargain
chapters.summary: Gussie and Nathaniel's POV alternating. He offers to move the press to a safe cellar; she realizes the price is his control of what gets printed. A charged, restrained moment between them by the frozen river. Emotional beat: love arriving disguised as an alliance, with terms attached.

chapters.title: The Raid That Missed
chapters.summary: Ellen's POV. Constables raid the wrong cellar; a printer's devil is arrested in Gussie's apron. Ellen covers for her, lying to a magistrate with steady eyes. Emotional beat: guilt — Gussie's risk has become other people's sacrifice.

chapters.title: What the Type Remembered
chapters.summary: Gussie's POV. Her father suffers a stroke at the composing stone. In his lucid hour he tells her to finish the mother's unfinished pamphlet — the one that names the mill owners' agent who provoked the lockout. Emotional beat: blessing and burden; the work is now truly hers.

chapters.title: The Agent's Name
chapters.summary: Gussie's POV. She verifies the pamphlet's claim against ledgers Nathaniel steals from his own master's office, learning he has been playing both sides. Emotional beat: disillusionment sharpened into resolve — she will use him as he used her.

chapters.title: Ten Pounds
chapters.summary: Ellen's POV. An informer in the relief committee sells a description: a young woman, ink-stained, left-handed. Ellen moves the press by barge skiff along the frozen canal at night. Emotional beat: fierce, unsentimental loyalty; the sisterhood of the type case.

chapters.title: The Trap on the Bridge
chapters.summary: Gussie's POV. The constables stake out the shop, guessing no one leaves the island without crossing. Nathaniel warns her — or leads her into it; she can no longer tell. Emotional beat: paranoia and tenderness colliding; trust as the last currency.

chapters.title: Setting the Last Page
chapters.summary: Gussie's POV. In the cellar, by candlelight, she sets the final page of her mother's pamphlet as the river ice begins to groan. Her father, half-paralyzed, guides her hand on the last line. Emotional beat: stillness before the storm; craft as devotion.

chapters.title: The Ice Breaks
chapters.summary: Multiple POVs converging. The thaw cracks the river; in the chaos of the breaking-up, the press run goes out by boat while constables storm the shop. Gussie stays behind to be found, the type scattered like shrapnel. Emotional beat: the climax — sacrifice staged as surrender.

chapters.title: The Magistrate's Room
chapters.summary: Gussie's POV. Interrogated, she says nothing; but the pamphlet is already in a thousand hands, and the agent's exposure forces an inquiry into the lockout. Nathaniel testifies, damning himself to save her. Emotional beat: justice arriving crooked, outside the law, paid for in ruin.

chapters.title: The Sentence
chapters.summary: Ellen's POV. Gussie is convicted of seditious libel — a fine and six months, light because the town's sympathy has turned. Ellen organizes the mill girls to pay the fine in coppers. Emotional beat: the movement, chastened, discovering its own strength.

chapters.title: Six Months of Winter
chapters.summary: Gussie's POV, in prison. She teaches inmates their letters, carving type from soap to show them how words are built. Nathaniel's letters arrive; her father's do not. Emotional beat: endurance transmuted into vocation; she has found the life invisibility was hiding.

chapters.title: The Atlas
chapters.summary: Gussie's POV, spring. Released, she returns to a reopened bridge and a shop that is now hers. She begins setting a new work — an atlas of the mill district, every street and strike and name, printed openly. Emotional beat: resolution — power reclaimed as memory, love chosen freely, justice written where the law can't erase it.
